public_rationale: Read plainly, 'cannot afford to pay anybody' means OpenAI lacked the money to pay its compute providers. The 2025 evidence says otherwise. FT-verified financials report that OpenAI paid Microsoft about $17.2 billion for cloud and R&D services in calendar 2025. In the week before the post, SoftBank also sent OpenAI a final $22-22.5 billion tranche. OpenAI's costs did far exceed its revenue ($34 billion spent against $13 billion of revenue), and investors filled that gap. If he meant OpenAI cannot pay from its own revenue, that narrower point holds. But that is a profitability claim, not an inability to pay. The 360-day CoreWeave terms he cites as proof could not be tied to OpenAI in a primary filing.
limitations: The figures come from leaked financials reported by the press, not published accounts.
The result depends on reading 'afford' as having the funds from any source.

'Afford' is read as having the funds available from any source (revenue or capital raised), not as covering costs from revenue alone. The narrower 'not from revenue' reading would make this a profitability claim, which is a separate claim in the post.
Target period: the claim describes an ongoing state with no named period, so it uses calendar 2025 up to the post date (2025-01-01 to 2025-12-29), the latest period public evidence covers.
The year-long CoreWeave terms are offered as an illustration. The test is whether OpenAI could pay providers.

criteria.contradiction_condition: Evidence that in 2025 OpenAI actually paid large compute bills and had substantial cash or capital available to pay providers.
